title: Venous Thromboembolism (DVT/PE): Pathogenesis, DOAC Revolution and Chronic Sequelae

content.intro: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) has a rich history dating back to ancient civilizations. The earliest recorded description of VTE was by Hippocrates in 460 BCE. However, it wasn't until the 19th century that the disease began to be understood. In 1856, German pathologist Rudolf Virchow described the triad of blood flow changes, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury that contributes to VTE. The discovery of heparin in 1916 by Jay McLean and the development of warfarin in 1940s revolutionized the treatment of VTE. The introduction of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) in the 2000s marked a new era in VTE management. Landmark papers, such as the 2004 paper by Schulman et al. on the use of fondaparinux for VTE treatment, have shaped our understanding of the disease.

Heparin was discovered in 1916 by Jay McLean
Schulman et al. published a landmark paper on fondaparinux in 2004
VTE understanding has evolved significantly over the centuries
Historical patients and outbreaks have contributed to our knowledge of VTE

lessons.title: Pathophysiology and Aetiology of Venous Thromboembolism

content.intro: VTE is a complex disease involving multiple molecular mechanisms and genetic factors. The coagulation cascade, which involves the interaction of various coagulation factors, plays a crucial role in VTE pathogenesis. Genetic factors, such as factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A mutations, can increase the risk of VTE. Subtypes of VTE, including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), have distinct pathophysiological mechanisms. The endothelium, platelets, and coagulation factors interact to form a thrombus, which can embolize and cause PE. Understanding the molecular mechanisms and genetic factors underlying VTE is essential for developing effective treatment strategies.

Genetic factors, such as factor V Leiden, increase VTE risk
Subtypes of VTE have distinct pathophysiological mechanisms
The endothelium, platelets, and coagulation factors interact to form a thrombus
Genetic factors can influence VTE risk
Coagulation factors, such as factor Xa, play a key role in VTE

content.intro: VTE can present with a range of symptoms, from asymptomatic to life-threatening. The cardinal symptoms of DVT include leg swelling, pain, and discoloration, while PE can present with sudden onset dyspnea, chest pain, and cough. Atypical presentations, such as phlegmasia cerulea dolens, can occur in rare cases. The clinical presentation of VTE can vary depending on the location and extent of the thrombus. Stages of VTE, including acute, subacute, and chronic, have distinct clinical features. Understanding the clinical presentation of VTE is essential for prompt diagnosis and treatment.
